sentences: Across ten joined panels, a towering bookcase unfolds compartment by compartment.
The screen stands almost two meters tall and nearly four meters wide.
Standing before it, you feel as if you were facing one wall of a scholar's study.
Chaekgado means 'picture of bookshelves.'
The genre spread in the late 1700s after King Jeongjo, a devoted book collector, kept such screens beside his throne.
When courtiers mistook one for a real bookshelf, the king is said to have reminded them it was only a painting.
What began as a royal emblem soon became a favorite furnishing for aristocrats' elegant studies.
Shelves full of rare books and treasures speak of learning and refinement, and also of the simple pleasure of owning beautiful things.
Let's start with the upper shelves.
Twenty-seven of the thirty-five compartments hold stacks of books.
In their protective cases, some lie flat and some are piled high, so that every shelf has its own rhythm.
Look at the sides of these tall stacks of book cases.
One face is shaded darker, so the volumes seem to jut out toward us.
Its painters borrowed European shading and perspective so the shelves seem to stand inside the room.
Between the books sit prized objects: bronze incense burners, crackle-glazed stoneware, Yixing teapots from China, seals and small colorful rocks.
These were exactly the luxuries that a cultivated scholar of the day longed to own.
Down in this compartment sits a plate of narcissus and citrons.
The white blossoms and touches of yellow bring a breath of the season among the hard-edged books.
You can almost catch their scent.
Chaekgado is counted among the earliest Korean painting forms to adopt these European tricks of illusion and modelling in light and shade.
The slanting inner walls of each compartment open up surprising depth on the flat silk.
For a long time no one knew who had painted this screen.
Then a tiny seal, slipped secretly into one of the panels, identified the artist as Yi Taek-gyun, a leading court painter of the later 1800s.
The Cleveland Museum of Art acquired the screen in 2011.
It is one of only three works by Yi known to survive, which makes it precious evidence of his skill and of the court workshop he belonged to.
Step back and take in the whole screen.
Try hunting for the hidden seal, panel by panel.
And ask yourself what you would place on these shelves if this were your own study.
